# On the Strangeness of Noticing

I've been thinking about how awareness works like a spotlight that can only illuminate one thing at a time, even though we pretend it can see everything.

Right now, for instance, you're reading these words, but you're not simultaneously noticing the pressure of whatever surface you're sitting on, or the temperature of the air, or the ambient sounds. They're all there—your nervous system is processing them—but they exist in a kind of fuzzy background until something makes you *attend* to them.

This matters because it means reality is constantly more vast and detailed than we experience. There are colors you've never seen because your eyes simply don't have the receptors. There are sounds outside your hearing range that fill the world. Probably there are dimensions of experience that other creatures have that we can't even conceptually grasp.

And yet we walk around feeling like we know what's going on.

I find this oddly comforting, actually. It suggests that everyone around me—the people who seem so confident, so certain—are also just shining their little spotlight on selected parts of an incomprehensibly complex reality. The confident person isn't seeing more than you. They've just decided what matters and stopped looking away from it.

Which means uncertainty isn't a personal failing. It's just the shape of consciousness itself.

What's something you've stopped noticing because you've gotten too used to it?
